title: CTI Tiers, IOCs vs TTPs & David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain
concept: Welcome to Stage B! Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) operates across three tiers: **Strategic** (high-level risk trends for executives/CISOs), **Operational** (campaign tracking & incoming attack context for IR leads), and **Tactical/Technical** (IOCs and detection engineering for SOC/SIEM). David Bianco's **Pyramid of Pain** ranks indicators by how costly it is for an adversary when defenders detect/block them—from bottom to top: (1) Hash Values (trivial—flip 1 byte!), (2) IP Addresses (easy), (3) Domain Names (simple), (4) Network/Host Artifacts (annoying—User-Agents, URI patterns, registry keys), (5) Tools (challenging—Cobalt Strike / phishing kit signatures), and (6) **TTPs** (Tough!—forcing the adversary to reinvent how they operate).
framework: Connects Intelligence Cycle (`intelligence-cycle`) with MITRE ATT&CK and Diamond Model.
caseStudy: In Case 06, moving up the Pyramid from a single C2 IP to HTTP favicon/TLS tool artifacts uncovered 14 sibling servers.
commonMistakes: Calling a raw list of 10,000 uncontextualized IP addresses 'threat intelligence'—that is merely a raw indicator feed!
legalNotes: Never block shared CDN/DNS IPs (like `8.8.8.8` or Cloudflare edge IPs) blindly from unvetted indicator lists.
notesPrompt: Draw the 6 layers of the Pyramid of Pain and give one real OSINT/SOC example for each layer.

quiz.prompt: Which CTI level (`_________`, Operational, or Tactical) is written for executives and CISOs making budget and risk decisions?
quiz.explanation: Strategic CTI informs high-level business, geopolitical, and architectural risk decisions.

quiz.prompt: What sits at the VERY BOTTOM of the Pyramid of Pain as the easiest indicator for attackers to change (`____` values)?
quiz.explanation: Recompiling or appending a single null byte completely changes a file's hash.

quiz.prompt: What sits at the VERY TOP of the Pyramid of Pain (`____`)?
quiz.explanation: Detecting TTPs forces adversaries to abandon core operational playbooks.

quiz.prompt: Who created the Pyramid of Pain in 2013? (Last name: `______`)
quiz.explanation: Detection engineer David Bianco authored the Pyramid of Pain.

quiz.prompt: What three-letter acronym (`___`) stands for Indicator of Compromise?
quiz.explanation: IOCs are technical forensic artifacts observed in or associated with intrusions.

title: Applying the Diamond Model & Cyber Kill Chain with OSINT
concept: When a SOC analyst receives a single suspicious domain or phishing attachment, the **Diamond Model** (`Adversary`, `Infrastructure`, `Capability`, `Victim`) provides a structured pivot map: starting at `Infrastructure` (domain -> RDAP -> passive DNS -> ASN -> TLS SANs), you pivot across to `Capability` (urlscan/VirusTotal observed scripts & malware hashes) and `Victim` (which industry brand is spoofed in the HTML `<title>`?). Pairing this with the **Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain** lets defenders sever attacks at Phase 1–3 (`Reconnaissance`, `Weaponization`, `Delivery`) before payloads execute.
framework: Directly operationalizes `diamond-model` and `kill-chain`.
caseStudy: Pivoting from one phishing URL (`Infrastructure`) to its login-kit JS hash (`Capability`) revealed simultaneous targeting of three regional telecoms (`Victim`).
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to naming a nation-state `Adversary` vertex when you only have uncorroborated `Infrastructure` and `Capability` data! Track unattributed clusters cautiously (e.g., `UNC-Cluster-04`).
legalNotes: Premature false attribution misleads leadership and risks public/legal fallout.
notesPrompt: Map a credential-harvesting phishing incident across all 4 Diamond Model vertices.

quiz.prompt: How many core vertices make up the Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis? (Type a number)
quiz.explanation: The four vertices are Adversary, Infrastructure, Capability, and Victim.

quiz.prompt: In the Diamond Model, malware families, exploits, and phishing kits belong to the `__________` vertex.
quiz.explanation: Capability represents the tools, exploits, and payloads wielded by the adversary.

quiz.prompt: In the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain, which phase (`Phase 1: ______________`) precedes Weaponization and Delivery?
quiz.explanation: Reconnaissance is Phase 1 of the Cyber Kill Chain.

quiz.prompt: What is Phase 6 of the Cyber Kill Chain (`_______ and Control` / `C2`)?
quiz.explanation: Command and Control (C2) establishes remote channel communication with compromised hosts.

quiz.prompt: When attribution is not yet proven, CTI teams group related intrusions under temporary activity `________` (e.g., `UNCxxxx`) rather than guessing an actor name.
quiz.explanation: Tracking unattributed intrusion clusters avoids premature attribution leaps.

title: Deep Dive: MITRE ATT&CK Reconnaissance (TA0043)
concept: MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise Tactic **TA0043 (Reconnaissance)** breaks pre-compromise information gathering into 10 core techniques (`T1589`–`T1598`): `T1595` Active Scanning, `T1592` Gather Victim Host Info, `T1589` Gather Victim Identity Info (credentials, email addresses, employee names), `T1590` Gather Victim Network Info (domain properties, DNS, IP blocks, network topology), `T1591` Gather Victim Org Info, `T1598` Phishing for Information, `T1597` Search Closed Sources, `T1596` Search Open Technical Databases (DNS/Passive DNS, WHOIS, Digital Certificates, CDNs, Scan Databases), `T1593` Search Open Websites/Domains, and `T1594` Search Victim-Owned Websites.
framework: Directly implements `mitre-attack-recon`.
caseStudy: Every Stage A module you mastered (Modules 9–16) maps 1-to-1 onto `T1589`, `T1590`, `T1591`, `T1593`, and `T1596`—showing how defenders audit their own exposure!
commonMistakes: Confusing `TA0043` Reconnaissance (pre-compromise external gathering) with `TA0007` Discovery (post-compromise internal network discovery after an attacker is already inside!).
legalNotes: Use MITRE ATT&CK TA0043 strictly for defensive exposure audits, purple-team detection mapping, and threat reporting.
notesPrompt: Explain the crucial boundary between MITRE `TA0043` (Reconnaissance) and `TA0007` (Discovery).

quiz.prompt: Which MITRE ATT&CK Tactic covers PRE-compromise external information gathering (`TA0043`: ______________)?
quiz.explanation: TA0043 Reconnaissance covers pre-compromise adversary intelligence gathering.

quiz.prompt: Which MITRE ATT&CK Tactic (`TA0007`: _________) covers POST-compromise internal enumeration AFTER initial access?
quiz.explanation: TA0007 Discovery occurs inside the environment post-compromise; TA0043 Reconnaissance occurs pre-compromise.

quiz.prompt: Searching Shodan, Censys, Passive DNS, WHOIS, and CT logs maps to MITRE Technique `T1596`: Search Open _________ Databases.
quiz.explanation: T1596 covers Search Open Technical Databases (.001 DNS/pDNS, .002 WHOIS, .003 Digital Certs, .005 Scan DBs).

quiz.prompt: Harvesting employee email naming patterns and job roles from public PDFs/socials maps to `T1589` (Gather Victim ________ Information).
quiz.explanation: T1589 covers Identity Information (.001 Credentials, .002 Email Addresses, .003 Employee Names).

quiz.prompt: Which web-based matrix tool (`ATT&CK _________`) colors and exports JSON technique layers for SOC coverage reviews?
quiz.explanation: MITRE ATT&CK Navigator visualizes and exports JSON TTP heatmaps.

title: Defensive Countermeasures & Attack Surface Reduction
concept: Because passive OSINT queries hit third-party databases (`crt.sh`, `archive.org`, `Shodan`), a firewall CANNOT 'block' someone from running passive recon! Instead, MITRE Mitigation **M1056 (Pre-compromise)** focuses on **Exposure Reduction**: (1) Strip EXIF/XMP metadata from public PDFs/media in CI/CD before publishing; (2) Use split-horizon DNS or wildcard TLS certs so internal hostname naming conventions don't leak into public CT logs; (3) Lock cloud origin servers behind CDN authenticated origin ACLs; (4) Reclaim dangling CNAMEs immediately; and (5) Scrub detailed software version stacks from public engineering job postings.
framework: Closes the loop from MITRE ATT&CK `TA0043` to defensive engineering (`M1056`).
caseStudy: Replacing per-host public certs on internal staging tools with private internal CA certs stopped new internal project codenames from leaking publicly on `crt.sh`.
commonMistakes: Expecting IDS/SIEM alerts to fire when an adversary conducts passive OSINT—passive recon leaves ZERO alerts in your SIEM!
legalNotes: Collaborate with HR, Legal, and DevOps when updating job-post templates and public document sanitization pipelines.
notesPrompt: Write a 5-point Organizational OSINT Exposure Hardening Checklist for a CISO.

quiz.prompt: Can a company's perimeter firewall detect or block an attacker querying `crt.sh` or Wayback Machine? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: Zero packets touch the company's network!
quiz.explanation: No—passive third-party queries never traverse the target's perimeter firewall.

quiz.prompt: Using an internal Private CA (instead of public CAs) for internal-only apps prevents internal hostnames from leaking into public __ logs.
quiz.explanation: Private Enterprise CAs are not required to log internal certificates to public Certificate Transparency logs.

quiz.prompt: Removing a forgotten CNAME record that points to an unclaimed cloud bucket prevents _________ takeover.
quiz.explanation: Cleaning up dangling CNAME/NS records prevents subdomain takeover attacks.

quiz.prompt: Overly detailed IT job listings ('Must manage Splunk 9.0.1 + Palo Alto PAN-OS 10.2 + Okta') inadvertently aid MITRE `T1592` / `T1591` tech-stack ______________.
quiz.explanation: Public job ads routinely disclose exact defensive vendor versions to adversaries.

quiz.prompt: Automating `exiftool -all=` inside web publishing pipelines mitigates public document ________ leaks.
quiz.explanation: Automated metadata scrubbing strips internal author usernames and file paths prior to public hosting.

title: Safe IOC Defanging & FIRST Traffic Light Protocol (TLP 2.0)
concept: Two operational safety standards govern every CTI team globally: (1) **Defanging**: before pasting any suspicious URL, domain, IP, or email into Slack, Jira, Google Docs, or SIEM notes, neutralize auto-linking (`https://bad.example.com` -> `hxxps://bad[.]example[.]com`, `198.51.100.9` -> `198.51.100[.]9`, `phish@bad.example` -> `phish[@]bad[.]example`) so no colleague or Slack link-preview bot accidentally visits the live attacker server! (2) **FIRST TLP 2.0** sharing designations: `TLP:RED` (named recipients only—zero forwarding), `TLP:AMBER+STRICT` (your organization ONLY), `TLP:AMBER` (your org + clients/partners who need to know to protect themselves), `TLP:GREEN` (broader security community, never public web), and `TLP:CLEAR` (unrestricted public).
framework: Governs Intelligence Cycle Step 5 (Safe Dissemination).
caseStudy: Pasting an undefanged spear-phishing URL into a team chat caused the chat server's link-preview bot to fetch the URL immediately, tipping off the threat actor!
commonMistakes: Using deprecated `TLP:WHITE` instead of `TLP:CLEAR`, or pasting live clickable URLs into messaging apps with automatic URL preview unfurling.
legalNotes: Violating a partner CERT's `TLP:RED` or `TLP:AMBER+STRICT` restriction destroys trust and can breach NDA/information-sharing agreements.
notesPrompt: Explain how chat-app 'link preview unfurling' creates a severe OPSEC leak if URLs aren't defanged.

quiz.prompt: How do you defang the period before a TLD in `evil.com`? (`evil___com`)
quiz.hint: Wrap the dot inside square brackets.
quiz.explanation: Square brackets `[.]` break clickable URL/domain auto-linking cleanly and reversibly.

quiz.prompt: Under FIRST TLP 2.0, which marking (`TLP:___`) restricts intelligence strictly to the individual named participants in a meeting/email?
quiz.explanation: TLP:RED is for the eyes and ears of named recipients only—no forwarding.

quiz.prompt: Under TLP 2.0, which modifier (`TLP:AMBER+______`) restricts sharing strictly inside the recipient's own organization (excluding clients)?
quiz.explanation: `TLP:AMBER+STRICT` limits sharing exclusively to the recipient organization.

quiz.prompt: Can `TLP:GREEN` advisories be posted publicly on open social media or indexed public blogs? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: TLP:GREEN is limited to the community, NOT public internet!
quiz.explanation: No—TLP:GREEN may be circulated among peers/community channels, but never posted on public web/socials (that requires TLP:CLEAR).

quiz.prompt: Which CyberChef operation (`______ URL`) automatically converts `https://...` into `hxxps://...[...]`?
quiz.explanation: CyberChef's `Defang URL` and `Defang IP Addresses` operations sanitize indicators instantly.

title: STIX 2.1, TAXII 2.1, MISP/OpenCTI & Feed Hygiene
concept: To share intelligence across thousands of organizations without manual CSV parsing, OASIS standardized **STIX 2.1** (JSON graph schema defining STIX Domain Objects like `Indicator`, `Threat-Actor`, `Intrusion-Set`, `Malware`, `Infrastructure`, `Vulnerability`, and STIX Relationship Objects like `indicates` or `uses`) and **TAXII 2.1** (the RESTful HTTPS API transport that serves STIX collections). Open-source platforms **MISP** and **OpenCTI** ingest, deduplicate, decay/expire stale indicators, and filter out 'poisoned' false positives (like major cloud DNS resolvers) before pushing high-confidence detections to a SIEM.
framework: Powers automated processing & dissemination in the Intelligence Cycle.
caseStudy: Setting an automated 14-day confidence decay TTL on dynamic VPS IP indicators prevented stale firewall blocks from breaking legitimate recycled cloud IPs months later.
commonMistakes: Blocking dynamic cloud IP indicators forever without an expiration/decay policy ('indicator aging').
legalNotes: Follow responsible coordinated vulnerability and threat disclosure channels via national CERTs/CSIRTs.
notesPrompt: Why do IP address IOCs decay (lose validity) much faster than malware TTP detections?

quiz.prompt: Between STIX and TAXII, which one is the HTTPS **transport protocol** (`_____`) rather than the JSON data schema?
quiz.hint: Think of a yellow cab carrying passengers!
quiz.explanation: TAXII is the transport API protocol that carries STIX JSON intelligence objects.

quiz.prompt: In STIX 2.1, `indicates`, `uses`, and `attributed-to` are examples of STIX ____________ Objects (SROs) connecting graph nodes.
quiz.explanation: STIX Relationship Objects (SROs) connect SDOs into an analytical knowledge graph.

quiz.prompt: Gradually lowering an IP indicator's score over days/weeks because cloud IPs get reassigned is called indicator _____ / aging.
quiz.explanation: Indicator decay/expiration prevents stale recycled cloud IPs from causing false-positive blocks.

quiz.prompt: Maintaining a list of untouchable domains/IPs (`google.com`, `1.1.1.1`, `microsoft.com`) so a bad feed never blocks business traffic is called a _______ list / allowlist.
quiz.explanation: MISP Warninglists prevent false-positive blocking of top Alexa/Tranco, CDN, and DNS infrastructure.

quiz.prompt: Which Swiss non-profit CTI project (`_____.ch`) publishes URLhaus, ThreatFox, and MalwareBazaar feeds?
quiz.explanation: abuse.ch provides high-signal, free community malware and C2 feeds.

title: SOC L1 Alert Triage & External OSINT Enrichment
concept: Inside a Security Operations Center (SOC), the **SIEM** (Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Elastic, Wazuh, QRadar) correlates internal logs (EDR process trees, DNS queries, firewall flows, proxy URLs, IAM logins). When an alert triggers, a **SOC Tier 1 Analyst** has minutes to answer: *True Positive, Benign True Positive (authorized scan/admin), or False Positive?* External passive OSINT enrichment supplies the missing context: (1) Domain registration age via RDAP (`<7 days` = high suspicion), (2) Passive DNS history & ASN (`residential CGNAT` vs `bulletproof VPS` vs `Microsoft Azure`), (3) GreyNoise scanner status, and (4) VirusTotal / ThreatFox / Pulsedive reputation.
framework: Unites Internal Telemetry + External OSINT inside the Traditional Intelligence Cycle.
caseStudy: In Case 07, GreyNoise + RIPEstat enrichment let a junior SOC analyst clear 118 benign internet-census alerts and escalate 2 real exploit attempts in 12 minutes.
commonMistakes: Looking ONLY at internal logs without enriching external destination domains/IPs—or conversely, trusting a `0/90` VirusTotal score as 'guaranteed safe' on a brand-new 10-minute-old spear-phishing link!
legalNotes: Never paste confidential internal employee usernames, hostnames, or session tokens into public external search boxes during enrichment!
notesPrompt: Write a 5-step SOC L1 External Enrichment Playbook for a suspicious outbound domain alert.

quiz.prompt: What four-letter platform (`____`) centralizes logs and generates correlation alerts inside a SOC?
quiz.explanation: A SIEM ingests, normalizes, and correlates security telemetry across endpoints, networks, and cloud.

quiz.prompt: Does `0 detections` on VirusTotal guarantee a brand-new 15-minute-old domain is benign? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: Brand-new zero-hour phishing domains haven't been reported to blocklists yet!
quiz.explanation: No—newly spun-up spear-phishing domains routinely show 0/90 detections initially; check RDAP creation age and DOM context.

quiz.prompt: Should a SOC analyst ever paste an internal Active Directory password or session JWT into a public OSINT search bar? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.explanation: Never—only query sanitized public indicators (IPs, external domains, file SHA-256 hashes).

quiz.prompt: An alert triggered by your own company's scheduled vulnerability scanner is classified as a ______ True Positive (`BTP`).
quiz.explanation: Benign True Positives reflect real activity caused by authorized admin or testing workflows.

quiz.prompt: Automating repetitive OSINT enrichment lookups via playbooks inside a SOC uses a `____` (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) workflow.
quiz.explanation: SOAR playbooks automatically enrich alert IPs/domains with RDAP, GreyNoise, and VT metadata.

title: Evaluating Reputation Scores, Sinkholes & CGNAT Pitfalls
concept: Experienced SOC analysts never take a single 'Malicious 85/100' score at face value—they read *why* an IP or domain was flagged: (1) **Security Sinkholes**: sometimes an infected workstation beacons to a malware domain whose DNS now resolves to `sinkhole.shadowserver.org` or a Microsoft/Kryptos Logic sinkhole IP—meaning the destination IP belongs to defenders, while your *internal workstation* is infected! (2) **Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) & Tor Exit Nodes**: blocking an entire mobile telecom `/16` block locks out thousands of legitimate customers; and (3) **Cloud Re-use**: an AWS EC2 IP malicious six months ago may belong to a harmless bakery today.
framework: Sharpens Analysis & Verification (Intelligence Cycle Step 4).
caseStudy: Recognizing a Shadowserver sinkhole PTR/RDAP record stopped a junior analyst from misreporting the sinkhole operator as 'an attacker scanning us' and redirected focus to cleaning the infected internal laptop!
commonMistakes: Treating outbound traffic to a known **security sinkhole IP** as 'harmless because a security company owns the IP'—NO! Outbound traffic to a malware sinkhole proves your internal machine tried to resolve a botnet C2 domain!
legalNotes: Document exact timestamps when correlating dynamic cloud or mobile CGNAT IPs.
notesPrompt: Explain why an internal host connecting outbound to a known Malware Sinkhole IP is an urgent endpoint infection sign.

quiz.prompt: If an internal workstation makes outbound requests to a known Malware ________ IP operated by researchers, is the internal workstation likely infected? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: Why would a laptop try to talk to a redirected botnet domain?
quiz.explanation: Yes! Malware sinkholes capture traffic destined for seized botnet C2 domains, proving the internal client attempted C2 contact.

quiz.prompt: What five-letter mobile/ISP NAT technology (`_____` — Carrier-Grade NAT) shares single public IPv4 addresses across thousands of mobile subscribers?
quiz.explanation: CGNAT shares public IPv4 pools across huge subscriber populations.

quiz.prompt: Which reverse DNS record type (`___`) resolves an IP address back to a hostname like `scanner-01.censys-scanner.com`?
quiz.explanation: PTR records provide reverse DNS hostnames that frequently identify scanners, CDNs, or sinkholes.

quiz.prompt: Can a cloud VM IP (AWS/DigitalOcean) that hosted malware 8 months ago belong to a completely benign customer today? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.explanation: Yes—always check `last_seen` timestamps in Passive DNS and threat feeds before judging cloud IPs.

quiz.prompt: In GreyNoise, what four-letter dataset name (`____`) identifies common benign business services (CDNs, DNS resolvers, update servers)?
quiz.explanation: GreyNoise RIOT ('Rule It OuT') catalogs trusted business and cloud infrastructure IPs.

title: Phishing Infrastructure Analysis with urlscan.io & Passive Artifacts
concept: Modern adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kits spin up disposable domains daily, yet reuse underlying templates, CSS/logo assets, exfiltration Telegram/webhook endpoints, and TLS provisioning scripts. Using **urlscan.io's passive search index** (`urlscan.io/search/`), IR analysts pivot without visiting live kits: search `page.title:"Sign in to your account" AND NOT page.domain:microsoft.com`, inspect `Files` tab SHA-256 hashes (`hash:<sha256>`) to find every other domain loading the exact same obfuscated JavaScript, and check `DOM` form `action=` endpoints to identify where stolen credentials are POSTed.
framework: Connects Diamond Model `Capability` (phishing kit JS) <-> `Infrastructure` (domains/IPs).
caseStudy: In Lab 25, a single custom CSS file hash on urlscan.io uncovered 20 active typosquatted login domains in under 60 seconds.
commonMistakes: Submitting a live spear-phishing URL that embeds `#victim.email@company.com` to a *Public* urlscan—leaking the victim's email to the entire internet and tipping off the phisher!
legalNotes: Strip any victim-identifying URL parameters/fragments and use Private/Unlisted sandboxes or passive search!
notesPrompt: List 4 pivotable artifacts visible inside an existing `urlscan.io` scan report.

quiz.prompt: What four-letter acronym (`____`) describes Adversary-in-the-Middle reverse-proxy phishing kits that steal session cookies alongside MFA codes?
quiz.explanation: AiTM phishing proxies relay real authentication flows to capture session cookies.

quiz.prompt: Before analyzing a phishing link, must you strip `#email` or `?user=` victim tokens so you don't leak employee PII or alert the attacker? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: Tokens uniquely identify which employee received the lure!
quiz.explanation: Always sanitize/redact victim-identifying query strings or URL fragments.

quiz.prompt: What Unicode-to-ASCII domain prefix (`__--`) signals an Internationalized Domain Name that could be a homograph spoof?
quiz.hint: Two letters followed by two hyphens.
quiz.explanation: `xn--` Punycode encoding exposes visually deceptive Unicode homograph domains.

quiz.prompt: In `urlscan.io` search syntax, `page._______:AS14061` filters historical scans hosted on a specific ASN.
quiz.explanation: `page.asn:` filters indexed scans by Autonomous System Number.

quiz.prompt: Checking which external URL receives the HTML `<form method="POST" action="...">` submission reveals the phishing kit's credential ____________ endpoint.
quiz.explanation: Inspecting POST/XHR exfiltration endpoints exposes attacker drop servers or bot webhooks.

title: Tracing Command & Control (C2) Clusters via JARM, TLS & Passive DNS
concept: During Incident Response, blocking the single C2 IP found in memory forensics rarely stops an intrusion if secondary backup C2 servers remain unblocked. IR analysts expand a single C2 indicator into a full cluster passively using: (1) **JARM TLS Fingerprints** (62-character fuzzy hash of how a server's TLS stack responds, pre-indexed in Shodan `ssl.jarm:` and Censys—note JARM identifies *software stacks* like Go/Python/Cobalt Strike defaults, so ALWAYS combine JARM with a second filter like ASN, port, or HTTP header to avoid false positives!), (2) **Default Self-Signed Cert Serials/Subjects**, and (3) **Passive DNS & Subnet Neighbors**.
framework: Executes Diamond Model Infrastructure-centered pivoting across Cyber Kill Chain Phase 6 (`C2`).
caseStudy: Combining a specific JARM hash + unusual TCP port + custom HTTP `404` byte length in Censys identified 9 backup C2 nodes before they were used.
commonMistakes: Blocking every IP matching a JARM hash alone! Because JARM fingerprints the underlying TLS library (e.g., standard Java or Go net/http), thousands of legitimate servers share the same JARM hash unless paired with cert/banner indicators.
legalNotes: Query pre-indexed JARM values inside Shodan/Censys passively rather than actively JARM-scanning third-party networks.
notesPrompt: Why must a JARM fingerprint ALWAYS be combined with additional banner/certificate attributes before blocking?

quiz.prompt: Is a matching JARM TLS hash ALONE sufficient proof that a server is malicious Cobalt Strike C2? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: JARM fingerprints the TLS stack/OS library, which legitimate apps also use!
quiz.explanation: No—JARM fingerprints TLS stack configurations (e.g., standard Java/Go), so always combine JARM with banner/cert/ASN corroboration.

quiz.prompt: What three-character TLS **client** fingerprint (`___`) hashes the `ClientHello` cipher/extension order sent by malware or browsers?
quiz.explanation: JA3 (and successor JA4) fingerprints outbound TLS ClientHello handshakes; JARM fingerprints TLS servers.

quiz.prompt: Which Shodan search filter (`ssl.____:`) queries pre-computed 62-character server TLS fingerprints?
quiz.explanation: `ssl.jarm:` searches Shodan's pre-indexed server TLS fingerprints passively.

quiz.prompt: Which abuse.ch platform (`_________`) specifically shares structured C2 IP:port and domain IOCs mapped to malware families?
quiz.explanation: abuse.ch ThreatFox catalogs actionable C2 indicators by malware family.

quiz.prompt: Checking whether `198.51.100.41` and `198.51.100.42` on the same VPS `/24` host identical unusual TLS certs is called subnet ________ pivoting.
quiz.explanation: Adversaries frequently provision multiple VPS nodes inside the same provider `/24` subnet.

title: Vulnerability Intelligence: CVE, CVSS, EPSS & CISA KEV
concept: Over 30,000 CVEs are published annually—no IT team can patch everything on Day 1. Vulnerability Intelligence combines four distinct open metrics: (1) **CVE** (standardized ID via MITRE/NVD), (2) **CVSS** (0.0–10.0 technical severity—note that many CVSS 9.8 bugs are *never* exploited in the wild!), (3) **EPSS** (FIRST's Exploit Prediction Scoring System, estimating 30-day real-world exploitation probability from `0.00` to `1.00`), and (4) **CISA KEV** (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities—confirmed active in-the-wild exploitation, including flags for `knownRansomwareCampaignUse`).
framework: Supports Cyber Kill Chain Phase 4 (`Exploitation`) defense and Risk-Based Prioritization.
caseStudy: In Lab 26, combining CISA KEV + EPSS 0.94 + external internet exposure prioritized a CVSS 7.5 edge VPN flaw ahead of an offline CVSS 9.8 lab bug.
commonMistakes: Patching strictly by `CVSS >= 9.0` while leaving internet-facing `CVSS 7.5` appliances listed on **CISA KEV** unpatched!
legalNotes: Reading public NVD, EPSS, and CISA KEV feeds is 100% open defensive intelligence.
notesPrompt: Write a 3-tier vulnerability prioritization formula combining CISA KEV, EPSS, CVSS, and Asset Exposure.

quiz.prompt: Does a high CVSS base score (e.g., `9.8`) automatically mean attackers are actively exploiting that CVE in the wild? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: CVSS measures theoretical technical severity, not active threat activity.
quiz.explanation: No—only a small fraction of high-CVSS vulnerabilities ever see active exploitation, which is why CISA KEV and EPSS matter.

quiz.prompt: Which field in the CISA KEV catalog explicitly warns defenders whether a CVE is used in `__________` campaigns?
quiz.explanation: CISA KEV includes `knownRansomwareCampaignUse` ('Known' / 'Unknown') to highlight severe extortion risk.

quiz.prompt: What organization (`_____`, Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) maintains both EPSS and TLP?
quiz.explanation: FIRST.org maintains CVSS, EPSS, and the Traffic Light Protocol (TLP).

quiz.prompt: What standardized naming scheme (`___` — Common Platform Enumeration) in NVD entries identifies exact affected vendor/product/version strings?
quiz.explanation: CPE strings (e.g., `cpe:2.3:a:vendor:product:version`) standardize software inventory matching.

quiz.prompt: Checking GitHub, Exploit-DB, and Nuclei templates to see if weaponized Proof-of-Concept (`___`) code is public helps gauge imminent scan surges.
quiz.explanation: Public weaponized PoC release typically triggers mass opportunistic exploitation within hours.

title: External Attack Surface Management (EASM) with Passive OSINT
concept: External Attack Surface Management (EASM) continuously repeats your Stage A passive workflow—`RDAP/ASN` + `crt.sh` + `Passive DNS` + `Wayback CDX` + `Shodan/Censys banners`—against **your own organization's authorized perimeter**. When a new critical CVE drops on Tuesday morning (e.g., affecting an SSL-VPN or file-transfer gateway), an analyst skilled in passive OSINT doesn't wait 48 hours for an internal vulnerability scan—they immediately query Censys/Shodan and CT logs for their own company's ASNs and subdomains to pinpoint every internet-exposed appliance in 90 seconds!
framework: Combines Stage A Passive Infrastructure (`Phase 4`) with Stage B Vulnerability Context (`Phase 7`).
caseStudy: Querying Censys across corporate ASNs uncovered a forgotten subsidiary VPN concentrator acquired in a merger two years earlier.
commonMistakes: Auditing only the main corporate domain (`company.com`) while forgetting acquired subsidiaries, regional TLDs, and shadow-IT cloud domains!
legalNotes: Always coordinate EASM inventories with asset owners and IT governance.
notesPrompt: Explain how M&A (mergers and acquisitions) create 'shadow attack surface' and how OSINT finds it.

quiz.prompt: What four-letter acronym (`____`) stands for External Attack Surface Management?
quiz.explanation: EASM continuously discovers and monitors internet-facing organizational assets.

quiz.prompt: Unapproved cloud servers or SaaS portals spun up outside central IT visibility are known as `______` IT.
quiz.explanation: Shadow IT assets frequently lack corporate EDR/patching until discovered via CT logs and passive DNS.

quiz.prompt: When a company acquires a startup, do the acquired startup's domains and ASNs expand the parent's external attack surface? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.explanation: Yes—mergers and acquisitions are a primary source of unmonitored external exposure.

quiz.prompt: Can passive Shodan/Censys banner version strings occasionally report false positives due to OS `___________` (where RedHat/Debian patch security bugs without bumping major version numbers)?
quiz.hint: Linux distros back-port fixes into stable version numbers (`back_______`).
quiz.explanation: Linux distributions backport security patches into stable version numbers, so confirm banner findings with internal package inventories.

quiz.prompt: Which Shodan alert feature monitors your own authorized CIDR netblocks passively for newly exposed ports (`Shodan _______`)?
quiz.explanation: Shodan Monitor notifies defenders when new banners or certs appear on their own netblocks.

title: Corporate OSINT: Statutory Registries, SEC EDGAR & GLEIF LEI
concept: Corporate investigations—vendor security vetting, M&A due diligence, fraud tracing, and supply-chain risk—rely on **statutory primary filings**, never unverified company 'About Us' marketing pages! Key pillars: (1) **National Registrars** (e.g., UK Companies House, SECP in Pakistan, ACRA in Singapore, Delaware Division of Corporations / State SOS portals), (2) **SEC EDGAR** (`10-K` annual reports, `EX-21` subsidiary disclosures, and `8-K Item 1.05` material cybersecurity incident reports), (3) **GLEIF (`search.gleif.org`)**—providing free 20-character ISO 17442 **LEI** codes with Level 2 parent-ownership trees, and (4) **OpenCorporates** for cross-jurisdictional officer/entity search.
framework: Maps to MITRE `T1591` (Org Information) and Due Diligence Verification.
caseStudy: In Case 08, GLEIF Level 2 parent trees + UK Companies House PSC records exposed hidden parent control behind a newly incorporated supplier.
commonMistakes: Confusing two completely unrelated companies that happen to share a similar trade name ('Apex Global Ltd' in two different countries) because you didn't record unique registration numbers / LEIs!
legalNotes: Always cite official Company Registration Numbers, jurisdiction codes, and filing dates.
notesPrompt: List what SEC Form `10-K`, `10-Q`, and `8-K Item 1.05` each disclose to an investigator.

quiz.prompt: In SEC EDGAR, which current-report form (`Form _-K`, Item 1.05) discloses material cybersecurity incidents at U.S. public companies?
quiz.explanation: SEC Form 8-K (Item 1.05) mandates timely public disclosure of material cybersecurity incidents.

quiz.prompt: On GLEIF (`search.gleif.org`), does `Level 2` data answer 'Who is who' or 'Who owns whom'? (`Who ____ whom`)
quiz.explanation: GLEIF Level 1 answers 'Who is who' (entity identity); Level 2 answers 'Who owns whom' (parent structures).

quiz.prompt: Why must corporate OSINT notes always record the statutory **Company Registration Number** alongside the company name? Because company names can ______ or collide across jurisdictions.
quiz.hint: Companies frequently rebrand/rename while keeping the same registration number!
quiz.explanation: Companies can change names multiple times, whereas their statutory registration number remains immutable.

quiz.prompt: Which global open database (`______________.com`) indexes over 200 million companies across 140+ jurisdictions?
quiz.explanation: OpenCorporates aggregates statutory company registration metadata globally.

quiz.prompt: Checking whether 45 shell companies share the exact same small suite address and incorporation agent tests registered-office _______ analysis.
quiz.explanation: Address and officer clustering distinguishes active operating businesses from mass formation-agent shells (note: legitimate law firms also host registered offices, so corroborate!).

title: Ultimate Beneficial Ownership (UBO) & Sanctions Screening
concept: In anti-money-laundering (AML), sanctions compliance, and supply-chain security, legal title often passes through multi-layered holding companies. Analysts trace upward from operating company -> intermediate holding company -> **Ultimate Beneficial Owner (UBO)** (for example, UK Companies House **Persons with Significant Control / PSC** holding `>=25%` shares or voting rights). Entities and officers are then screened against consolidated enforcement lists (**OFAC SDN**, **UN Security Council**, **EU Financial Sanctions**, **UK OFSI**) via **OpenSanctions**, carefully matching transliterations, Dates of Birth, and corporate registration IDs to prevent false-positive name collisions.
framework: Supports high-rigor Corporate & Compliance Intelligence.
caseStudy: Matching exact passport/DOB and corporate tax numbers in OpenSanctions eliminated 14 innocent namesake matches while confirming 1 sanctioned subsidiary.
commonMistakes: Flagging an innocent person on a sanctions list based on a common first+last name match without verifying DOB, nationality, and secondary identifiers!
legalNotes: Compliance findings require legal review; never publish uncorroborated sanctions allegations publicly.
notesPrompt: Explain the difference between a nominee/corporate director and an Ultimate Beneficial Owner (UBO).

quiz.prompt: What three-letter acronym (`___`) stands for Ultimate Beneficial Owner—the natural person who ultimately owns or controls an entity?
quiz.explanation: Ultimate Beneficial Owners (UBOs) are the natural persons holding ultimate ownership or control.

quiz.prompt: In UK Companies House PSC rules, holding more than `__`% of shares or voting rights triggers mandatory PSC disclosure.
quiz.explanation: Holding >25% of shares or voting rights triggers UK Person with Significant Control (PSC) reporting.

quiz.prompt: Which U.S. Treasury office (`____`) publishes the Specially Designated Nationals (`SDN`) sanctions list?
quiz.explanation: OFAC (Office of Foreign Assets Control) administers U.S. economic sanctions and the SDN list.

quiz.prompt: What open compliance database (`_____________.org`) consolidates OFAC, UN, EU, UK, and PEP datasets?
quiz.explanation: OpenSanctions unifies international sanctions and PEP lists with structured entity schemas.

quiz.prompt: Spelling variations across alphabets (e.g., Arabic, Cyrillic, Urdu, or Mandarin names rendered in Latin script) are known as name ________________.
quiz.explanation: Accounting for phonetic transliteration variants is essential in global corporate and sanctions research.

title: Advanced Attribution Standards, Circular Reporting & Anti-Doxxing
concept: When investigations involve human actors—whether corporate fraudsters, disinformation networks, or public-interest accountability subjects—evidentiary thresholds must be at their absolute highest. Three non-negotiable standards: (1) **Defeat Circular Reporting**: trace every secondary claim back to its *primary root* to ensure two sources aren't quoting the same origin; (2) **Multi-Anchor Corroboration**: require independent convergence across statutory records, cryptographic/domain artifacts, and chronological alignment; and (3) **Strict Anti-Doxxing Redaction**: never expose residential addresses, private family members, medical data, or personal ID numbers.
framework: Implements Admiralty Code source independence rules.
caseStudy: In Lab 28, tracing hyperlinks revealed three articles all echoed one 4-hour-old homoglyph parody account.
commonMistakes: Counting 5 news reposts of the exact same wire story or anonymous tweet as '5 independent sources'—that is still ONLY 1 source!
legalNotes: Strict compliance with GDPR/privacy law, anti-harassment law, and newsroom/corporate legal review is mandatory before any external publication.
notesPrompt: Draw a diagram showing True Independent Triangulation vs Single-Origin Circular Reporting.

quiz.prompt: If 10 blogs reprint the exact same unverified anonymous forum post, how many genuinely independent primary sources do you actually have? (Type a number)
quiz.hint: All 10 point to the same single origin!
quiz.explanation: Reprints of a single origin equal at most 1 uncorroborated source (circular reporting).

quiz.prompt: Should family members or minors ever be included in an OSINT investigation report? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: Zero public interest and severe privacy harm.
quiz.explanation: Never—uninvolved family members and minors are strictly off-limits.

quiz.prompt: Archiving screenshots WITH full browser URL bar, UTC clock, and SHA-256 hash preserves evidentiary _____ of custody.
quiz.explanation: Documented Chain of Custody ensures evidence is reproducible and defensible.

quiz.prompt: Giving subjects of public-interest investigative journalism a fair opportunity to respond prior to publication is called Right of _____.
quiz.explanation: Right of Reply is a cornerstone ethical safeguard in investigative journalism—often uncovering context that corrects errors before publication.

quiz.prompt: Separating 'What we observed directly' from 'What we infer it means' prevents analytical ____.
quiz.explanation: Explicitly separating observed facts from analytical assessments prevents hidden bias.

title: Transition Boundary: Passive OSINT vs Ethical Primary Outreach
concept: In journalism and corporate compliance (unlike zero-touch SOC passive recon), authorized workflows sometimes conclude with transparent, on-the-record outreach (such as a journalist requesting official comment or a vendor auditor requesting a SOC 2 certificate). Understand the bright boundary: transparent professional inquiry identifies who you are honestly, whereas **social engineering / pretexting** (lying about your identity to trick a helpdesk or target into revealing private data) is deceptive, often illegal (e.g., Gramm-Leach-Bliley / fraud statutes), and **strictly forbidden** in ethical OSINT.
framework: Clarifies the boundary between OSINT and HUMINT / Social Engineering.
caseStudy: A journalist completed 100% of passive archival preservation BEFORE sending an official right-of-reply email—so the subject could not quietly delete archived web pages afterward!
commonMistakes: Contacting a subject for comment *before* archiving all public web evidence—prompting immediate mass deletion of public pages!
legalNotes: Never engage in deceptive pretexting or unauthorized social engineering.
notesPrompt: Why must 100% of passive archival collection finish BEFORE any authorized external inquiry occurs?

quiz.prompt: Calling a bank or helpdesk pretending to be someone else to extract private info is deceptive `__________` (strictly forbidden in OSINT).
quiz.explanation: Pretexting is deceptive social engineering—illegal in many contexts and never part of ethical OSINT.

quiz.prompt: In investigative journalism, must you complete all passive archiving BEFORE sending a Right-of-Reply inquiry? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: Subjects often delete posts immediately upon learning of scrutiny!
quiz.explanation: Yes—reaching out alerts the subject, so preserve public archives and hashes first.

quiz.prompt: When a researcher identifies themselves truthfully and asks an agency press office a question on the record, that crosses from passive OSINT into transparent primary ________.
quiz.explanation: Transparent on-the-record inquiry is overt outreach—only done when authorized by scope.

quiz.prompt: In a SOC/Threat Intel passive investigation, should an analyst EVER email or message a suspected threat actor? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: Destroys OPSEC and violates SOC RoE!
quiz.explanation: Never—engaging threat actors compromises OPSEC, tips off adversaries, and violates enterprise security policy.

quiz.prompt: Protecting confidential whistleblowers and sources from metadata/IP exposure is known as ______ protection.
quiz.explanation: Source protection requires strict metadata scrubbing and encrypted channels.

title: Conceptual Architecture: Surface Web, Deep Web & Dark Web
concept: Media headlines constantly confuse the **Deep Web** and the **Dark Web**. Let's establish exact technical definitions (concepts only—no access instructions): (1) **Surface Web (Clearnet)**: public HTTP/HTTPS pages indexed by Google/Bing; (2) **Deep Web**: >90% of the normal internet—every legitimate page NOT indexed by search engines (your Gmail inbox, university ERP, online banking, hospital portals, paid academic journals, private corporate databases); (3) **Dark Web**: a tiny fraction of the Deep Web built on encrypted **overlay networks** (most notably Tor's onion routing, I2P, or Freenet) using cryptographic special-use domains (`.onion`, RFC 7686). Note that onion routing itself was created for communications privacy and hosts legitimate newsrooms (BBC, NYT, ProPublica, Deutsche Welle) and whistleblower dropboxes alongside illicit sites.
framework: Provides accurate threat-landscape literacy for Strategic & Operational CTI.
caseStudy: In Lab 29, distinguishing ordinary Deep Web SaaS portals from Dark Web `.onion` leak blogs prevented sensationalized executive reporting.
commonMistakes: Calling a password-protected clearnet database or unlisted Telegram channel 'the Dark Web'!
legalNotes: This module teaches conceptual architecture ONLY. Never browse illicit markets, never interact with threat actors, and strictly follow national laws and corporate legal policies.
notesPrompt: Write a crystal-clear 3-row table contrasting Surface Web, Deep Web, and Dark Web for non-technical executives.

quiz.prompt: Does your private online banking dashboard on standard HTTPS belong to the `Deep Web` or the `Dark Web`?
quiz.explanation: Authenticated, unindexed standard web portals make up the Deep Web.

quiz.prompt: Which IETF RFC (`RFC ____`) officially reserved the `.onion` special-use domain name?
quiz.explanation: RFC 7686 designates `.onion` as a special-use domain not resolved via standard public DNS.

quiz.prompt: Is every `.onion` service illegal? (Answer yes or no—think of BBC, NYT, and SecureDrop whistleblower portals)
quiz.hint: Major newsrooms and civil-society organizations operate legitimate .onion mirrors.
quiz.explanation: No—onion routing is a dual-use privacy technology used by major newsrooms, researchers, and activists.

quiz.prompt: Can standard recursive DNS (`8.8.8.8`) resolve `.onion` addresses directly? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: RFC 7686 explicitly excludes .onion from standard DNS.
quiz.explanation: No—standard DNS resolvers return NXDOMAIN for `.onion` per RFC 7686.

quiz.prompt: In onion routing, traffic passes through multiple encrypted relay hops (Entry Guard -> Middle Relay -> ____ Relay) for clearnet destinations.
quiz.explanation: Exit relays forward clearnet-bound traffic; `.onion` internal rendezvous circuits stay entirely inside the overlay.

title: Safe Clearnet Threat Monitoring & Strict Legal Boundaries
concept: How do enterprise SOC and CTI analysts stay informed about ransomware group claims or credential-exposure campaigns **without** exposing corporate networks, breaking laws, or visiting illicit infrastructure? Through **vetted Clearnet CTI Feeds & CERT Advisories**: national CSIRTs, CISA/ENISA joint advisories, MISP/OpenCTI community feeds, Have I Been Pwned domain alerts, Abuse.ch, and accredited threat-intelligence providers that extract sanitized **metadata** (targeted sector, CVE exploited, MITRE TTPs, C2 hashes) onto standard HTTPS APIs. Analysts NEVER pay threat actors, NEVER download contraband/stolen dumps, and ALWAYS involve Legal Counsel & Law Enforcement when data-extortion claims arise.
framework: Enforces Legal & Governance gates across Stage B CTI.
caseStudy: When a supplier's name appeared on a public ransomware tracker metadata feed, the SOC immediately audited VPN logs and rotated partner API keys without ever touching illicit infrastructure.
commonMistakes: Curiosity-browsing criminal sites from a corporate or home machine—exposing the analyst to malware exploits, OPSEC deanonymization, and severe legal liability!
legalNotes: Never access illegal content, never download stolen data dumps, and always escalate suspected extortion incidents immediately to Legal Counsel and Incident Response leadership.
notesPrompt: List four safe clearnet sources that provide actionable ransomware/malware TTP intelligence legally.

quiz.prompt: Should a junior SOC analyst ever browse illicit underground sites from their corporate workstation? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: Massive legal, malware, and policy violation!
quiz.explanation: Never—rely on sanitized clearnet CTI feeds, CERT advisories, and authorized legal/IR channels.

quiz.prompt: When a third-party vendor suffers a suspected ransomware event, what defensive action on YOUR network (`rotate` keys / audit logs) takes immediate priority?
quiz.explanation: Auditing B2B VPN/SSO logs and rotating shared API credentials contains supply-chain blast radius immediately.

quiz.prompt: Do joint CISA / FBI / NCSC ransomware advisories publish actionable MITRE ATT&CK TTPs and IOCs on the clearnet for free? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.explanation: Yes—official `#StopRansomware` advisories publish verified TTPs, IOCs, and detection rules openly.

quiz.prompt: Should an OSINT analyst ever communicate with, bait, or negotiate with an extortion actor? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: Strictly restricted to specialized legal/IR crisis negotiators.
quiz.explanation: Never—unauthorized engagement creates severe operational, legal, and sanctions risks.

quiz.prompt: Before acting on a threat actor's boast that they 'hacked Company X', remember threat actors frequently lie or recycle old public data—grade unverified actor boasts as low ____________ until corroborated!
quiz.explanation: Adversary claims are routinely exaggerated or fabricated for extortion leverage.

title: Structured Analytic Techniques (SATs), Cognitive Biases & ACH
concept: The greatest point of failure in OSINT is rarely a missing tool—it is the human brain's cognitive shortcuts! Four biases trap investigators daily: (1) **Confirmation Bias** (seeking only clues supporting your hunch), (2) **Anchoring Bias** (fixating on the first IP/suspect mentioned), (3) **Mirror-Imaging** (assuming an actor in another context thinks just like you), and (4) **Availability Heuristic** (blaming whichever APT group was in yesterday's headlines). Richards Heuer's **Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH)** defeats these traps: list ALL plausible hypotheses across columns (`H1`, `H2`, `H3`, including `H0: Benign/Coincidence`), list diagnostic evidence down rows, and score **inconsistencies** (`I` vs `C`)—the strongest hypothesis is the one with the *fewest refuting inconsistencies*, NOT the most cherry-picked confirmations!
framework: Elevates OSINT Cycle Step 4 (Analysis) to professional intelligence tradecraft.
caseStudy: In Case 10, an ACH matrix refuted hasty nation-state attribution by proving Cyrillic HTML comments came from a 6-year-old public website template.
commonMistakes: Using an ACH matrix only to tally confirming checkmarks (`C`) instead of focusing on **diagnostic refuting evidence (`I` / Inconsistent)**!
legalNotes: Documenting competing hypotheses and dissenting evidence protects organizations from costly misjudgments.
notesPrompt: Build a mini 3-hypothesis ACH table (`H1 Targeted Phish`, `H2 Authorized Pentest`, `H3 Misconfigured Marketing Domain`).

quiz.prompt: Who authored *Psychology of Intelligence Analysis* and formalized Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH)? (Last name: `_____`)
quiz.explanation: Richards J. Heuer Jr. formalized ACH in *Psychology of Intelligence Analysis*.

quiz.prompt: In ACH, is the winning hypothesis the one with the most confirmations, or the one with the FEWEST refuting _______________?
quiz.explanation: Following Karl Popper's falsification principle, ACH eliminates hypotheses contradicted by diagnostic evidence.

quiz.prompt: Assuming a threat actor or foreign organization shares your exact mindset and habits is called `______`-imaging bias.
quiz.explanation: Mirror-imaging projects the analyst's own cultural/operational logic onto others.

quiz.prompt: If a piece of evidence is equally consistent (`C`) with EVERY hypothesis (`H1`, `H2`, and `H3`), how much diagnostic value does it have for separating them? (`____` / none)
quiz.hint: It doesn't distinguish between any of the rivals!
quiz.explanation: Evidence consistent with all hypotheses has zero diagnostic power to differentiate them.

quiz.prompt: Should an ACH matrix always include a 'Benign / Misconfiguration / Coincidence' null hypothesis? (Answer yes or no)
quiz.hint: Hanlon's Razor: misconfigurations happen every day!
quiz.explanation: Yes—routine IT misconfigurations frequently mimic suspicious anomalies.

title: Admiralty Source Grading, Estimative Language & BLUF Reports
concept: Your investigation only creates value if a busy editor, SOC manager, or CISO can act on your report in 60 seconds! Professional OSINT reports follow five structural rules: (1) **TLP Marking** at top & bottom (`TLP:CLEAR`, `TLP:AMBER`, etc.); (2) **BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front)**—lead with Key Judgment + **Confidence Level** (`High`, `Moderate`, `Low`) + **Words of Estimative Probability** (`Almost Certain` ~95%, `Likely` ~70%, `Roughly Even Chance` ~50%, `Unlikely` ~20%); (3) **Admiralty Code (`A–F` × `1–6`)** grading every key source & claim independently; (4) **Evidence & Methodology Body** with defanged IOCs, UTC timestamps, archival permalinks, and SHA-256 hashes; and (5) **Intelligence Gaps & Recommendations** (explicitly stating what remains unknown!).
framework: Master capstone of `admiralty-code` and Intelligence Cycle Dissemination.
caseStudy: Grading an anonymous account's geolocated video as `F1` (Unknown source reliability `F`, independently confirmed solar/satellite truth `1`) communicated crystal-clear nuance to decision-makers.
commonMistakes: Burying the conclusion on page 8 of a chronological tool diary ('First I ran whois, then I ran dig...') instead of opening with a crisp BLUF!
legalNotes: Defang all malicious indicators (`hxxps://`, `[.]`), state TLP clearly, and separate observed facts from estimative judgments.
notesPrompt: Write a model 4-sentence BLUF executive summary using estimative probability, confidence level, and Admiralty code.

quiz.prompt: In the Admiralty Code (`A–F` and `1–6`), what does letter `F` stand for regarding Source Reliability? ('Reliability ______ be judged')
quiz.explanation: `F` means Source Reliability cannot be judged (e.g., a brand-new or anonymous source).

quiz.prompt: In the Admiralty Code, what does number `1` stand for regarding Information Credibility? ('_________ by other independent sources')
quiz.hint: Nine-letter past participle starting with Conf...
quiz.explanation: `1` means Confirmed by independent sources (such as mathematical geolocation or cryptographic CT logs).

quiz.prompt: Can a report say 'High Confidence that X is Unlikely'? (Answer yes or no—Confidence measures evidence quality, Likelihood measures probability!)
quiz.hint: Strong evidence proving something won't happen = High Confidence it is Unlikely!
quiz.explanation: Yes! Confidence reflects the strength of your evidence base, whereas Estimative Probability expresses likelihood.

quiz.prompt: Should a professional report explicitly include an 'Intelligence ____' section stating what you still do NOT know?
quiz.explanation: Stating Intelligence Gaps honestly prevents decision-makers from over-assuming coverage.

quiz.prompt: Passing the Stage B Final Exam (>=70%) awards the 'Advanced OSINT & ______ Intel Certificate'.
quiz.explanation: Completing Stage B earns the Advanced OSINT & Threat Intel Certificate.
